title: The CCPR of Teacher Credibility
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that a teacher new to a building lacks credibility, and that this is the first thing students, coworkers and bosses are quietly judging. He warns that campaigning for credibility with showy classroom success stories backfires, and instead boils credibility down to care, competence and passion. Care must cover both the student as a person and the student as a learner, a gap he admits he fell into as a new teacher. Competence comes from daily determination to learn something new, and passion from loving students, content and the craft that joins them. He adds a fourth letter, Repair, noting that offensiveness is a distinctive credibility killer, so teachers should watch their humor and apologize earnestly when a student seems offended.
points: Credibility is earned through care, competence and passion rather than announced through staff-meeting boasting.
Caring about students personally is not enough; students must also see that you care about them learning, or they will not rate you a good teacher.
The one shortcut to competence is to arrive each day determined to learn something new and to treat today's failures as fertile ground.
Offensiveness, even accidental, damages credibility sharply, so teachers should be careful with humor and watch for students whose behavior turns negative.
Repair, an earnest hallway apology, is the fourth element that restores credibility after a misstep.
quotes: Starting out at a new school is hard, whether you’ve got no years of experience or ten. You can bring instructional expertise, nuclear passion, and tomes of knowledge, but when you start at a new school, there’s a big thing you lack: credibility.

So they’re trying to figure out if you’re credible. That’s why people treat you weirdly when you’re starting out at a new place. And the bad news is that it’s not super effective to go around trying to explicitly convince them of your credibility.
The good news is that credibility can actually be boiled down pretty succinctly. Students (and coworkers and bosses) determine a teacher’s credibility based on CCP: care, competence, and passion.

When I was a new teacher, I was huge on caring about the kids personally, but I was terrible at demonstrating my concern that they learn as much as possible about reading, writing, and thinking in my class. To my students, I’m sure that they found me a nice person, even a good person — but I’m also sure that many of them did not find me a particularly good teacher.

There aren’t many shortcuts to competence, but here’s one: every day, go in to work determined to learn something new. If you’re currently bad at your job (I was), then I’ve got good news: you’ll fail today, and that failure is ripe ground for learning.

But some years ago, researchers found that there’s a particular form of misbehavior that can tank your credibility no matter how good you are: offensiveness. When we offend our students, whether intentionally or not, researchers find that our credibility takes a deadly hit.

One implication of this is that we’re wise to be careful with our humor. Another is that we need to keep an eye out for student behaviors that shift from positive to negative, and act like detectives when this happens to try to determine if we may have accidentally offended the student.
